title: Provide WHO-prequalified dengue vaccination for defined endemic populations

concept.text: Reduce dengue disease and hospitalization through vaccination in populations with a favorable benefit–risk balance. Qdenga achieved WHO prequalification; protection and safety across baseline serostatus and individual serotypes remain important limits. Proposed completion test: WHO prequalification and recommendation for a specified endemic population, supported by a large randomized phase 3 trial measuring virologically confirmed dengue and hospitalization, with analyses by baseline serostatus. Test set by: WHO; its programme recommendation targets children aged 6–16 years in high-transmission settings. Reported achieved: Qdenga received WHO prequalification on 9 May 2024. Earlier, FDA approved Dengvaxia on 1 May 2019 for a restricted previously infected population. Overlaps: VIR-04. Sources given: [WHO Qdenga prequalification record](https://extranet.who.int/prequal/vaccines/p/qdengar) ; [WHO dengue vaccination recommendations and limitations](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/dengue-vaccines) ; [FDA Dengvaxia approval record](https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/dengvaxia) ; [Anvisa on Butantan-DV registration and safety investigation](https://www.gov.br/anvisa/pt-br/assuntos/noticias-anvisa/2026/vacina-da-dengue-do-instituto-butantan-nao-e-experimental).

page.title: WHO-prequalified dengue vaccination for endemic populations
page.definition: A dengue vaccine meets WHO prequalification requirements for use in a WHO-recommended endemic population, where dengue transmission persists. Prequalification assesses vaccine quality, safety, efficacy and suitability for United Nations procurement.

goal.need: WHO’s 2024 surveillance recorded dengue cases and deaths across all six WHO regions. The reported totals below quantify disease that prevention programmes seek to reduce. WHO recommends TAK-003 vaccination for children aged 6–16 years in settings with high dengue transmission intensity.

figures.caption: Dengue reported to WHO worldwide in 2024.
figures.note: Surveillance counts; severe cases and deaths are included in the reported case burden.

statements.quote: WHO recommends the use of TAK-003 in children aged 6–16 years in settings with high dengue transmission intensity.

statements.body: WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization
statements.quote: there is an urgent need to develop dengue vaccines, especially to protect people from disease in endemic countries.

completion.title: WHO prequalifies a dengue vaccine for use in a population it recommends vaccinating.
completion.criterion: A dengue vaccine enters WHO’s List of Prequalified Vaccines after positive assessment of quality, safety, efficacy and programme suitability, with a WHO recommendation specifying its endemic population and schedule. Met by Qdenga (TAK-003): its prequalification record gives an effective date of 9 May 2024. WHO recommends two doses at least 3 months apart for children aged 6–16 years in high-transmission settings.
completion.set_by: World Health Organization, vaccine prequalification programme and dengue vaccination recommendations.
completion.threshold_quote: meets WHO standard for vaccine quality, safety and efficacy standards, as endorsed by the WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization (ECBS)
completion.basis: This capability is achieved for WHO’s specified programme population. Prequalification establishes acceptability in principle for United Nations procurement. WHO does not recommend programmatic TAK-003 use in low-to-moderate transmission settings while its efficacy–risk profile against serotypes 3 and 4 in people without previous dengue infection requires further assessment.

milestones.title: A dengue vaccine induces neutralizing antibodies to all four virus types in non-human primates.
milestones.criterion: Use the published seroconversion endpoint: a reciprocal PRNT50 titre ≥10 and a ≥4-fold rise from baseline. PRNT50 is the serum dilution reducing infectious-virus plaques by 50%; dengue virus types are termed serotypes. The developers’ 2011 review reproduces testing of three formulations in groups of 8 cynomolgus macaques. At day 91, one formulation produced seroconversion rates of 87.5%, 100%, 100% and 100% against serotypes 1–4. These are observed proportions, not a prescribed minimum success rate.
milestones.set_by: Inviragen and CDC investigators, published nonclinical seroconversion endpoint reproduced in Table 5 of the developers’ 2011 review; WHO identifies responses to all four serotypes as a development objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: Seroconversion: defined as PRNT ≥10 and ≥4-fold increase in PRNT50 over day 0 baseline titer.

milestones.title: A dengue vaccine completes 28-day safety follow-up after each dose in a registered phase 1 trial.
milestones.criterion: In NCT01224639, healthy adults aged 18–45 years receive a dengue vaccine, with injection-site and systemic reactions assessed for 28 days after each vaccination. The 2014 report describes 96 randomized adults: 79 received DENVax and 17 placebo. Investigators reported no vaccine-related serious adverse events; 47 of 76 evaluable vaccine recipients seroconverted to all four serotypes 30 days after dose 2. Absence of such events was an observed result, not a universal phase 1 licensing threshold.
milestones.set_by: Takeda’s registered phase 1 protocol NCT01224639, as described by its investigators in the primary publication.
milestones.threshold_quote: Primary endpoints were frequency and severity of injection-site and systemic reactions within 28 days of each vaccination.

milestones.title: A dengue vaccine passes a safety-board gate before younger cohorts enter a phase 2 trial.
milestones.criterion: NCT01511250 requires safety-board approval of 28-day data from the first 12 participants in a cohort before further enrolment and initiation of the next younger cohort. Conducted between November 2011 and April 2016, the phase 2 study enrolled sequential age groups from 21–45 years down to 1.5–5 years, followed by a paediatric expansion. It randomized 360 participants overall, including 148 in the antibody-response component. At month 4, 87% of vaccine recipients in the full analysis set were antibody-positive to all four serotypes.
milestones.set_by: Inviragen/Takeda protocol NCT01511250 and its independent data safety monitoring board, as described in the published phase 2 study.
milestones.threshold_quote: These data were evaluated by the data safety monitoring board and once approved, the remaining participants were enrolled in group 1

milestones.title: A dengue vaccine’s phase 3 efficacy has a lower 95% confidence bound above 25%.
milestones.criterion: TIDES (NCT02747927) requires the lower 95% confidence bound for efficacy against symptomatic, viral-RNA-confirmed dengue of any serotype to exceed 25%. Children aged 4–16 years receive two doses 3 months apart; the primary window starts 30 days after dose 2 and ends at the 12-month follow-up. The 2019 report describes 20,099 randomized participants and 19,021 in the per-protocol analysis. Efficacy was 80.2% (95% CI 73.3–85.3), with 61 vaccine-group cases and 149 placebo-group cases.
milestones.set_by: Takeda’s registered TIDES protocol NCT02747927, prespecified primary efficacy success criterion described in the primary publication.
milestones.threshold_quote: met if the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for vaccine efficacy was above 25%.

milestones.title: A dengue vaccine obtains marketing authorization for a defined age group.
milestones.criterion: A competent regulator grants marketing authorization with an approved population and schedule. The European Commission authorized Qdenga throughout the European Union on 5 December 2022, following EMA assessment. Its approved indication covers prevention of dengue disease from 4 years of age; the schedule is two doses 3 months apart, with use according to official recommendations.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Qdenga marketing authorization; approved indication and schedule published by the European Medicines Agency.
milestones.threshold_quote: Qdenga is indicated for the prevention of dengue disease in individuals from 4 years of age.

milestones.title: WHO recommends a dengue vaccine for children aged 6–16 years in high-transmission settings.
milestones.criterion: WHO recommends TAK-003 in two doses at least 3 months apart for children aged 6–16 years. Indicators of high transmission include dengue-antibody prevalence >60% by age 9 years or mean age of peak dengue hospitalizations <16 years. TIDES follow-up, completed by 18,257 participants about 4.5 years after dose 2, found cumulative efficacy from dose 1 of 61.2% (95% CI 56.0–65.8) against confirmed dengue and 84.1% (77.8–88.6) against hospitalization. In participants uninfected before vaccination, efficacy against serotype 3 was not observed; serotype 4 incidence was insufficient for evaluation.
milestones.set_by: World Health Organization, population recommendation stated in its 15 May 2024 prequalification announcement and subsequent dengue-vaccine guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: WHO recommends the use of TAK-003 in children aged 6–16 years in settings with high dengue burden and transmission intensity.

not_found: No universal numerical pass/fail cutoff for phase 1 or phase 2 safety was found in WHO’s dengue-vaccine guidance.
The original 2011 macaque-study article could not be opened; the developers’ review reproduces its seroconversion definition and results.
WHO’s English position-paper PDF of 3 May 2024 could not be opened; its population recommendation was verified in WHO’s accessible guidance.
EMA’s initial Qdenga assessment report could not be opened; authorization and indication were verified in its overview and product information.

results.finding: In NCT01511250, 148 participants entered four age-descending groups after safety-board review of each cohort’s first 12 participants.
results.detail: The board approved 28-day safety data before further enrollment and initiation of the next younger group.
results.quote: These data were evaluated by the data safety monitoring board and once approved, the remaining participants were enrolled in group 1, concurrently with the first 12 participants in group 2; this system of enrollment was maintained for all 4 study groups.

results.finding: TIDES TAK-003 trial: 19,021 per-protocol participants; efficacy lower 95% confidence bound was 73.3%.
results.detail: Children aged 4–16 received two doses three months apart. The primary endpoint covered 11 months beginning 30 days after the second dose; there were 61 vaccine-group and 149 placebo-group cases.
results.quote: The primary endpoint was achieved with an overall vaccine efficacy of 80·2% (95% CI 73·3 to 85·3; 61 cases of VCD in the TAK-003 group vs 149 cases of VCD in the placebo group).

results.finding: WHO recommends TAK-003 for children aged 6–16 years in high-transmission settings; sample size not applicable.
results.detail: WHO specifies a 2-dose schedule with a 3-month interval. The source also identifies seroprevalence above 60% by age 9 as a potential indicator of high transmission; it does not report the TIDES follow-up results.
results.quote: WHO recommends the use of TAK-003 in children aged 6–16 years in settings with high dengue burden and transmission intensity. The vaccine should be administered in a 2-dose schedule with a 3-month interval between doses.

results.finding: In 20,071 trial participants, TAK-003 efficacy against confirmed dengue was 61.2%; 18,257 completed follow-up.
results.detail: The trial also found 84.1% efficacy against hospitalisation. Among initially seronegative participants, efficacy against DENV-3 was not observed and DENV-4 incidence was too low to evaluate. The source does not report the specified WHO recommendation.
